subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: A student tests a food sample with Benedict's solution and heats it in a water bath. It stays blue. This shows the food:
options: Contains a lot of reducing sugar
questions.explain: Benedict's solution stays blue when no reducing sugar is present; it turns green, yellow, orange or brick-red if sugar is present.

questions.q: In the food test, what colour does Benedict's solution turn when heated with a reducing sugar?
questions.explain: Benedict's solution turns from blue to brick-red/orange when a reducing sugar is present.

questions.q: What colour change shows a positive result when iodine solution is added to a food containing starch?
questions.explain: Iodine solution turns from orange-brown to blue-black in the presence of starch.

questions.q: Which nutrient is the body's main source of energy?
questions.explain: Carbohydrates are the primary energy source in a balanced diet.

questions.q: Enzymes speed up reactions but are not used up themselves. This means an enzyme can:
options: Only be used once and then destroyed
Be reused to catalyse the reaction many times
questions.explain: As catalysts, enzymes are not used up in the reaction and can be used again and again.

questions.q: Which food test uses Biuret solution turning from blue to purple?
questions.explain: Biuret solution turns purple/lilac in the presence of protein.

questions.q: On a graph of rate against temperature, why does the rate fall sharply after the optimum temperature?
options: The enzyme starts to work faster
The enzyme is denatured and the active site changes shape
questions.explain: Above the optimum, high temperature denatures the enzyme, changing the active site so the rate falls.

questions.q: What happens to a digestive enzyme if the pH is far from its optimum?
options: It turns into a different enzyme
Its active site changes shape (denatures) and it stops working
questions.explain: Extremes of pH denature an enzyme by changing the shape of its active site so the substrate no longer fits.

questions.q: Why does breaking large food molecules into smaller ones help the body?
options: Small soluble molecules can be absorbed across the gut wall into the blood
questions.explain: Digestion makes molecules small and soluble enough to be absorbed into the bloodstream.

questions.q: Why does a very high or very low pH usually stop an enzyme working?
options: It changes the shape of the active site, denaturing the enzyme
It gives the enzyme more energy
It turns the enzyme into a product
questions.explain: Extreme pH alters the active site's shape (denaturation) so the substrate no longer fits.

questions.q: Which statement about bile is correct?
options: It is an enzyme that digests fat
It breaks protein into amino acids
It is made in the pancreas
It emulsifies fats and neutralises stomach acid
questions.explain: Bile is not an enzyme; it emulsifies fat and is alkaline so it neutralises acid from the stomach.

questions.q: What happens to an enzyme when it is heated well above its optimum temperature?
options: Its active site changes shape and it is denatured
questions.explain: High temperatures denature enzymes by changing the active site's shape; enzymes are not alive so cannot be 'killed'.

questions.q: Why does the large intestine play a role at the end of digestion?
options: It absorbs water from undigested food to form faeces
It absorbs amino acids into the blood
questions.explain: The large intestine absorbs water, leaving solid faeces to be egested.

questions.q: Why must a Biuret test for protein be carried out without heating, unlike the Benedict's test?
options: Because protein is destroyed by Benedict's solution
Because protein only forms in the cold
Because heating turns all proteins into sugars
Because the Biuret test gives its colour change at room temperature
questions.explain: The Biuret test produces a purple/lilac colour at room temperature, so heating is not required (unlike Benedict's test for sugars).

questions.q: The optimum temperature for most human enzymes is about:
questions.explain: Most human enzymes work best at around body temperature, 37°C.

questions.q: As temperature increases up to the optimum, the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction:
options: Increases because particles collide more often with more energy
questions.explain: Up to the optimum, higher temperature increases kinetic energy and collision frequency, raising the rate.

questions.q: Which combination of food test and positive result is correct?
options: Iodine solution turns from orange-brown to blue-black with starch
Biuret solution turns brick-red with protein
Benedict's solution turns purple with starch
questions.explain: Iodine solution changes from orange-brown to blue-black in the presence of starch.

questions.q: Which type of enzyme are amylase and other carbohydrases?
questions.explain: Enzymes are proteins that act as biological catalysts.

questions.q: Which food test uses Benedict's solution, and what positive result shows?
options: Test for sugar (reducing sugar); turns from blue to brick-red/orange on heating
Test for lipid; forms a milky emulsion
questions.explain: Benedict's solution, heated, turns from blue to brick-red/orange when a reducing sugar is present.

questions.q: A lipid molecule is made up of:
options: One sugar and one amino acid
Three fatty acids and one glycerol
questions.explain: A lipid (fat or oil) is made of three fatty acid molecules joined to one glycerol molecule.

questions.q: The 'lock and key' model explains that an enzyme:
options: Has an active site with a specific shape that fits a particular substrate
questions.explain: The active site has a complementary shape to its specific substrate, like a key fitting a lock.

questions.q: Why does emulsifying fat by bile speed up its digestion?
options: It increases the surface area of fat for lipase to act on
It absorbs the fat into the blood
Bile chemically digests the fat itself
questions.explain: Bile breaks large fat droplets into smaller ones, giving lipase a larger surface area to work on.
